title: SMTP Service Extensions for Transmission of Large and Binary MIME Messages
summary: Defines two SMTP extensions: one lets large messages be sent in chunks, and the other allows binary MIME content without needing to encode it as text. This makes mail transfer of big or binary messages simpler. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: SMTP normally ends a message with a line holding a single dot, and both sides have to scan the whole message looking for it. This RFC adds a command that states the exact length of the data that follows, so large messages need no scanning. It also lets a sender send binary content without the text encoding that would otherwise inflate it.

questions: how to send binary mime over smtp
subtitle: Two SMTP extensions: send mail in length-prefixed chunks with BDAT, and send raw binary MIME with no text encoding.

tldr.problem: The DATA command ends a message with a line containing only a dot, so both ends have to scan the message for that sequence, and the sender has to say how much data is coming only by ending the transfer. Sending binary attachments also costs a base64 or quoted-printable encoding that inflates the message.
tldr.mechanism: The CHUNKING extension adds a BDAT command whose first argument is the exact length in octets of the data that follows, with an optional LAST marker. The BINARYMIME extension adds a BODY=BINARYMIME value to MAIL, which tells the receiver to preserve every bit in each octet.
tldr.outcome: Large messages can be sent and counted without scanning for the end of data, and binary MIME content can travel unencoded between hosts that support it. The RFC obsoletes RFC 1830.

facts.label: BDAT syntax
facts.value: BDAT SP chunk-size [ SP end-marker ] CR LF

today: RFC 3030 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2000. It obsoletes RFC 1830, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Two Extensions
sections.content:
The MIME extensions to the Internet message format provide for the transmission of many kinds of data that were previously unsupported in Internet mail. Anticipating the need to transport the new media more efficiently, the SMTP protocol has been extended to provide transport for new message types. RFC 1652 defines one such extension for the transmission of unencoded 8-bit MIME messages, allowing the receiver SMTP to declare support for 8-bit body parts and the sender to request 8-bit transmission of a particular message.

One expected result of the use of MIME is that the Internet mail system will be expected to carry very large mail messages. In such transactions there is a performance-based desire to eliminate the requirement that the message be scanned for "CR LF . CR LF" sequences upon sending and receiving, to detect the end of the message.

Independent of the need to send large messages, Internet mail is increasingly multimedia. There is a need to avoid the overhead of base64 and quoted-printable encoding of binary objects sent using the MIME message format over SMTP between hosts that support binary message processing.

The memo uses the mechanism defined in RFC 1869 to define two extensions to the SMTP service, whereby a receiver SMTP may declare support for the message chunking transmission mode and for the reception of Binary messages, which the sender SMTP is then free to use. The Working Group Summary records that the protocol in RFC 1830 was classified as experimental at the time because of questions about the robustness of the Binary Content-Transfer-Encoding in the MIME implementations of the day, and that as MIME has matured and other uses of that encoding have been deployed, those concerns have been allayed.
sections.plainLanguage: SMTP normally ends a message with a line holding a single dot, and both sides have to scan the whole message looking for it. This RFC adds a command that states the exact length of the data that follows, so large messages need no scanning. It also lets a sender send binary content without the text encoding that would otherwise inflate it.

sections.title: The CHUNKING Extension and the BDAT Command
sections.content:
The CHUNKING service extension is defined with the name "CHUNKING" and the EHLO keyword value "CHUNKING". A new SMTP verb, BDAT, is defined as an alternative to the DATA command of RFC 821. It takes two arguments: the length in octets of the binary data chunk, and an optional second argument indicating that the data chunk is the last. The syntax is bdat-cmd ::= "BDAT" SP chunk-size [ SP end-marker ] CR LF, chunk-size ::= 1*DIGIT and end-marker ::= "LAST". Servers that offer the BDAT extension MUST continue to support the regular DATA command.

When a sender wants to send a large message using the extension, it first issues EHLO. If the receiver replies with code 250 and the response includes the EHLO keyword value CHUNKING, the receiver is saying it supports BDAT and will accept messages in chunks. After all MAIL and RCPT responses are collected and processed, the message is sent as a series of BDAT commands. The message data is sent immediately after the trailing CR LF of the BDAT command line, and once the receiver has the specified number of octets it returns a 250 reply code.

The optional LAST parameter marks the last chunk of message data. The last BDAT command MAY have a byte count of zero, indicating there is no additional data. Any BDAT command sent after the BDAT LAST is illegal and MUST be replied to with a 503 "Bad sequence of commands" reply code; the resulting state is indeterminate and a RSET command MUST be sent to clear the transaction before continuing. A 250 response MUST be sent to each successful BDAT data block. If a failure occurs after a BDAT command is received, the receiver MUST accept and discard the associated message data before sending the appropriate 5XX or 4XX code. If the receiver has declared support for command pipelining, it MUST be prepared to accept and discard additional BDAT chunks already in the pipeline after the failed one.

The RFC adds two notes about failure. An error on the receiver such as a full disk can only be reported after the BDAT segment has been received, so it is important to choose a reasonable chunk size given the expected end-to-end bandwidth. And because the receiver does not acknowledge the BDAT command before the message data is sent, it is important to send BDAT only to systems that have declared the capability: sending it to a non-CHUNKING capable system will make the receiver parse the message data as if it were a very long ESMTP command line containing binary data.

DATA and BDAT commands cannot be used in the same transaction. If a DATA statement is issued after a BDAT for the current transaction, a 503 "Bad sequence of commands" MUST be issued, the state is indeterminate, and a RSET must clear the transaction. There is no prohibition on using DATA and BDAT in the same session, so long as they are not mixed in the same transaction.

The RFC also explains why chunking helps with counting. The local storage size of a message may not accurately reflect the actual size of the message sent, due to local storage conventions, and text messages sent with BDAT MUST be sent in the canonical MIME format with lines delimited by CR LF. It may not be possible to convert the entire message to canonical form at once, and CHUNKING provides a mechanism to convert the message to canonical form, accurately count the bytes, and send the message a single chunk at a time.

Correct byte counting is essential. If the sender indicates a chunk size larger than the actual chunk, the receiver will wait for the remainder of the data, or, when streaming, will read the subsequent command as additional message data, and the parser will return a syntax error when the incomplete command is read. If the sender indicates a chunk size smaller than the actual chunk, the receiver will interpret the remainder of the message data as invalid commands, and the remainder may be binary, so lexicographical parsers MUST be prepared to receive, process and reject lines of arbitrary octets.
sections.plainLanguage: The new command is BDAT, and it says how many bytes follow before the bytes start. The receiver counts them off and replies once the block has arrived. The sender marks the final block with the word LAST, and may use a count of zero for it. The command can only be used with servers that have advertised it.

sections.title: The BINARYMIME Extension
sections.content:
The BINARYMIME service extension is defined with the name "BINARYMIME" and the EHLO keyword value "BINARYMIME". It can only be used with the CHUNKING service extension, no parameter is used with the keyword, and no new verbs are defined for it. It may be used for SMTP message submission.

RFC 1652 defines the BODY parameter for the MAIL command, and this extension adds a value to it, "BINARYMIME", so that the body-value syntax becomes body-value ::= "7BIT" / "8BITMIME" / "BINARYMIME". The value indicates that the message is a Binary MIME message, in strict compliance with MIME, with arbitrary octet content being sent. The maximum length of a MAIL FROM command line is increased by 16 characters by the possible addition of the BODY=BINARYMIME keyword and value.

A sender may request that a binary MIME message be sent without transport encoding by sending a BODY parameter with the value BINARYMIME with the MAIL command. When the receiver accepts a MAIL command with that body-value, it agrees to preserve all bits in each octet passed using the BDAT command. Once a receiver supporting BINARYMIME accepts a message containing binary material, it MUST deliver or relay the message in such a way as to preserve all bits in each octet.

BINARYMIME cannot be used with the DATA command. If a DATA command is issued after a MAIL command containing the body-value of BINARYMIME, a 503 "Bad sequence of commands" response MUST be sent, the resulting state is indeterminate, and the transaction MUST be reset with RSET. It is especially important when using BINARYMIME to ensure that the MIME message itself is properly formed, and in particular that text is canonically encoded with each line properly terminated with CR LF. Any transformation of text into non-canonical MIME to observe local storage conventions MUST be reversed before sending as BINARYMIME, and text/* MUST be sent with CR LF terminated lines. Although CR and LF do not necessarily represent ends of text lines in BDAT chunks, the RFC 2781 prohibition against using a UTF-16 charset within the text top-level media type remains.

If a receiver does not indicate support for the BINARYMIME message format, the sender MUST NOT, under any circumstances, send binary data. If the receiver does not support BINARYMIME and the message is a MIME object with a binary encoding, the sender has three options. It may implement a gateway transformation to convert the message into valid 8-bit MIME, if the receiver supports the 8BITMIME transport extension and the content is amenable to being encoded in 8 bits. It may implement a gateway transformation to convert the message into valid 7-bit MIME. Or it may treat this as a permanent error and handle it in the usual manner for delivery failures. The conversion is constrained in two ways: it must cause no loss of information, with MIME transport encodings employed as needed to ensure that, and the resulting message must be valid 7-bit or 8-bit MIME, so the transformation must not result in nested Base64 or Quoted-Printable content-transfer-encodings. The RFC notes that at the time of writing there are no mechanisms for converting a binary MIME object into an 8-bit MIME object, since that would require a new MIME content-transfer-encoding.

Finally, if the MIME message contains a Binary content-transfer-encoding and the BODY parameter does not indicate BINARYMIME, the message MUST be accepted and SHOULD be returned to the sender with an appropriate delivery status notification.
sections.plainLanguage: The second extension adds the word BINARYMIME to the BODY parameter of the MAIL command. When the receiver accepts that value, it promises to deliver the message without changing a single bit. The sender must not use it unless the receiver advertised the keyword, and it cannot be combined with the ordinary DATA command.

sections.title: The Two Dialogues
sections.content:
Section 4.1 of the RFC shows a simple chunking exchange that sends a short pseudo-RFC 822 message to one recipient. The client opens the connection, the server answers 220, the client sends EHLO and the server replies with 250 and the keyword CHUNKING. The client then sends MAIL FROM and RCPT TO, which are each accepted, and finally BDAT 86 LAST followed by the three header lines of the message. The server replies 250 Message OK, 86 octets received.

Section 4.2 shows a BINARYMIME object sent to two recipients using the CHUNKING and PIPELINING extensions. The server's greeting lists PIPELINING, BINARYMIME and CHUNKING. The client sends MAIL FROM:<ned@ymir.claremont.edu> BODY=BINARYMIME and the two RCPT commands without waiting for replies in between, which is what pipelining allows. The server answers all three with 250.

The client then sends BDAT 100000 with the first 10000 octets of canonical MIME message data, and later BDAT 324 with the remaining 324 octets, and finally BDAT 0 LAST to mark the end. The server replies 250 for each chunk and finally 250 Message OK, 100324 octets received, which is the sum of the two chunk sizes.
sections.plainLanguage: The first dialogue sends a short message in one block. The second sends a binary message to two recipients, and splits it into two blocks with a final empty block marked LAST. The receiver's last reply gives the total number of octets it accepted.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that the extension is not known to present any additional security issues not already endemic to electronic mail and present in fully conforming implementations of RFC 821, or otherwise made possible by MIME.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says the extension raises no security issues beyond those that email already has.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 1830
sections.content: Appendix A of the RFC lists the changes from RFC 1830. There were numerous editorial changes, including required intellectual property boilerplate and revised authors' contact information. The simple chunking example was corrected to use the correct number of bytes, and the pipelining example was updated to illustrate the BDAT 0 LAST construct.
sections.plainLanguage: This edition is the same protocol as the experimental one, with the text tidied up and the examples corrected.

viz.caption: THE SIMPLE CHUNKING EXAMPLE FROM SECTION 4.1

data.title: One chunk, one recipient
data.code:
R: 220 cnri.reston.va.us SMTP service ready
S: EHLO ymir.claremont.edu
R: 250-cnri.reston.va.us says hello
R: 250 CHUNKING
S: MAIL FROM:<Sam@Random.com>
R: 250 <Sam@Random.com> Sender ok
S: RCPT TO:<Susan@Random.com>
R: 250 <Susan@random.com> Recipient ok
S: BDAT 86 LAST
S: To: Susan@random.com<CR><LF>
S: From: Sam@random.com<CR><LF>
S: Subject: This is a bodyless test message<CR><LF>
R: 250 Message OK, 86 octets received
S: QUIT
R: 221 Goodbye
